Reddit (RDDT) is back in focus after the company reported third quarter earnings on October 29, 2026, along with fresh fourth quarter revenue guidance and an update on its ongoing share repurchase program.

Reddit's latest earnings and buyback update hit a stock that has been under pressure for much of 2026, with the share price climbing 1.38% on the day and 4.54% over the past week but still down 40.53% on a 30 day share price return basis and 60.68% year to date, while the 1 year total shareholder return has fallen 53.43%. This signals short term momentum around results against a backdrop of weaker longer run performance.

Scan beyond Reddit's sharp drawdown and see how other beaten up but financially solid companies compare by running the 40 high quality undervalued stocks alongside this latest earnings and buyback story.

Reddit now appears to be a business posting solid revenue and profit figures, even though the stock has been hammered this year. After that sharp drawdown and modest rebound, is the current price actually fair value for what you get?

Most Popular Narrative: 78% Undervalued

The narrative fair value for Reddit of $423.68 sits far above the latest close at $95.10, which puts the spotlight firmly on why such a wide gap exists according to John_Eric, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who built this valuation and wrote the narrative that underpins it.

But past 60%, something flips. A discount that big is more often a sign my model is missing something than a sign the market is wrong. The market doesn't usually hand out fifty-plus percent off a genuinely good business for no reason, so before that number pulls me in, I go find the reason. If I can't find one, I assume I built the model wrong before I assume I found a once-in-a-decade gift.

See why 19 investors see Reddit as 78% undervalued.

Result: Fair Value of $423.68 (UNDERVALUED)

Still, the Reddit story could be knocked off course if the Google content standoff breaks against the platform or if US user engagement weakens further from here.

Find out about the key risks to this Reddit narrative.

Another View: Reddit Through The P/E Lens

There is a different read on Reddit when you look purely at earnings multiples. The stock trades on an 18.5x P/E, which is roughly double the US Interactive Media and Services sector at 9x, yet below the peer average of 37.2x and under the fair ratio of 27.1x that the market could move towards. That mix of richer pricing than the wider industry but cheaper terms than close comparables leaves a real question for investors. Is this a mispriced growth story or simply a premium that needs more proof to hold?

Reddit COO Says "Over 80% of Our Monetization" Is Logged In. Google Is Squeezing the Rest ©@Brett Jordan from Pexels via Canva; @Corina Ciocirlan's Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Reddit stock closed at $95 on Friday, down 37% in three months and just above its 52-week low.

Third-quarter revenue rose 53% to $895 million, but CEO Steve Huffman warned daily users could fall by a low double-digit percentage.

COO Jen Wong says logged-in users drive over 80% of monetization, and those users are still growing.

At about 11x forward earnings with $3 billion of net cash, Reddit's February 5 report is the next test.

Reddit (RDDT:NYSE) closed at $95 on Friday, down 37% over three months and only about 7% above its 52-week low of $89.

The trouble comes from Alphabet (GOOGL:NASDAQ). Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode answer more questions on Google's own pages, and Reddit says that cut its search referrals by more than 1 million a week in October.

Pinterest (PINS) sold off the same day after its third-quarter revenue grew just 12% and missed its own outlook. Reddit grew more than four times as fast, yet it now trades at about 11x forward earnings.

Strong quarter, shrinking audience

The third quarter was strong:

Revenue up 53% to $895 million, above the $878 million consensus

Net income of $283 million, or $1.40 per share, up 74%

Free cash flow of $363 million, nearly double a year earlier

Revenue is up about 2.6 times in two years…

Reddit (RDDT): total revenue, quarterly, $ millions, Q3 2024–Q3 2026 (TIKR)

The warning came with the guide. Fourth-quarter revenue is guided to $1.00 billion to $1.03 billion, up 38% to 42%, and the midpoint sits below the roughly $1.05 billion consensus.

Huffman also said daily active uniques could fall by a low double-digit percentage from about 130 million if search referrals keep sliding.

The users who pay are still here

Most of the lost traffic is logged out: people who land from a Google search, read one thread and leave.

Those visitors earn Reddit very little. As COO Jen Wong put it on the call, "Over 80% of our monetization sits on the shoulders of logged-in in-app users."

So Reddit is leaning into that base. It plans to test a primarily logged-in experience in select markets outside the U.S. this quarter, and it's already testing ad placements in its search pages.

Its margins give it room to experiment. Compare them with Pinterest's:

Reddit's adjusted EBITDA margin hit 45% last quarter, and the guide implies about 49% for the fourth.

title: If You're Trying To Become A Day Trader, There Are Some Problems Nobody Warns You About. And They Have Nothing To Do With Reading Charts

If You're Trying To Become A Day Trader, There Are Some Problems Nobody Warns You About. And They Have Nothing To Do With Reading Charts
Analyst analyzing charts on screen (Credit: Photo: Shutterstock)

RDDT

Learning how to read charts, spot patterns and time trades might seem like the hardest part of becoming a day trader. But one trader with more than six years of experience says the real challenges often come later, when emotions start getting in the way of making good decisions.

In a recent Reddit discussion, the experienced trader shared seven common mistakes that can wipe out a trading account. Although trading hasn't become a full-time income, it has helped pay for family vacations and home renovations. And the trader has learned that understanding the market is only part of the battle.

Don't Miss:

Texas Is Adding 440+ Data Centers. There's A Problem: They All Need Power. One Houston Developer Is Building New Natural Gas Plants To Meet That Demand.

Luxury Hotel Supply Is Growing 4 Times Slower Than Global Wealth. Here's What's Driving The Growing Gap.

The Biggest Mistakes Have Nothing To Do With Charts

One of the first problems is how differently people react to winning and losing. If losing $1,000 hurts more than making $1,000 feels good, the trader says that's a warning sign.

Another trap is becoming obsessed with recovering losses. Someone who starts with $10,000 and drops to $9,000 might suddenly take bigger risks just to get back to where they started.

"Sometimes you need to cut off a finger to save the hand," the trader wrote.

There's also the problem of forgetting how much you've already made. Someone who turns $1,000 into $10,000 and then loses $3,000 might feel devastated, even though they're still $6,000 ahead.

But perhaps the biggest mistake is selling winning trades too early while holding losing positions for too long, hoping they'll eventually recover.

Trending: Think Your IRA Can Only Hold Stocks And Funds? Think Again. Here's What A Self-Directed IRA Can Actually Invest In.

One commenter knew that struggle well.

"I am very disciplined with my stop loss and never hold losers past my stop," they wrote. "But I always exit winners too early."

Another trader described getting caught up in recovering losses and increasing their position sizes on poor setups.

"Now it's 3 losses and I'm done for the day no matter where I'm at," they wrote.

Can You Really Learn To Trade Without Risking Real Money?

The original poster also warned against obsessing over missed opportunities and constantly wondering what would have happened if you'd made a different decision.

But the most controversial advice was to avoid paper trading altogether. The trader believes practicing with fake money doesn't prepare people for the emotional pressure of losing real money.

Pinterest CEO: The EU Hit Was "Greater Than We Anticipated." Its Q4 Guide Sits $70 Million Light ©buchachon from Getty Images and Roberto Nickson from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Pinterest closed at $18.96, down 19% in three months, near the $18.17 average price it paid for more than $2 billion of buybacks.

Third-quarter revenue grew 12% to $1.17 billion, missing its own guidance after EU rule changes cut cross-border seller ad spending.

Reddit plunged about 30% the same day after warning that Google's AI search is cutting its traffic, while Pinterest's users hit a record.

Pinterest's early February report must show fourth-quarter revenue near the top of its $1.425 billion to $1.475 billion guide.

Pinterest (PINS:NYSE) closed Friday at $18.96, down 4.2% on the day and 19% over three months. Earlier this year, it spent more than $2 billion buying back stock at an average of $18.17.

Oct. 30 hit two social platforms hard. Reddit (RDDT:NYSE) plunged about 30% after warning that Google's AI search features are cutting its referral traffic, while Pinterest slid on a revenue miss and a weak holiday guide.

The problems aren't the same. Reddit is losing visitors, with U.S. daily users down 2% to 50.7 million. Pinterest set a user record, and its weak spot was advertisers in Europe.

A customs rule cost three points

CEO Bill Ready blamed the European Union's removal of its de minimis exemption on low-value imports, which led cross-border sellers to cut ad spending. "The regulatory impact was greater than we anticipated," he said on the earnings call.

That pullback took about 3 points off global growth. The rest of the damage:

Revenue rose 12% to $1.17 billion, below Pinterest's own $1.19 billion to $1.21 billion range.

Europe revenue was flat at $193 million, with cross-border sellers an 11-point drag.

Adjusted EPS of $0.46 missed the $0.49 estimate.

Quarterly sales make the stall easy to spot…

Pinterest (PINS): total revenue, quarterly, $ billions, Q3 2024–Q3 2026 (TIKR)

Third-quarter revenue slipped below the second quarter's $1.18 billion, an unusual dip heading into the holidays.

Record users, flat monetization

Monthly active users reached a record 661 million, up 10%, with rest of world growing fastest. Revenue grew only a bit faster, so revenue per user barely moved.

Reddit shows the mirror image. Its revenue jumped 53% to $895 million even as U.S. users fell.

The fourth-quarter guide reflects Pinterest's strain. It expects revenue of $1.425 billion to $1.475 billion, up 8% to 12%, against a $1.52 billion consensus. Adjusted EBITDA is guided to $538 million to $588 million, below the $611.8 million estimate.

title: Reddit’s (RDDT) Short-Term Pains May Lead to Long-Term Gains
detail:
Reddit’s (RDDT) Short-Term Pains May Lead to Long-Term Gains

Reddit's (RDDT) short-term pains may lead to long-term gains, in my view. The leading social media platform lost more than 25% of its market value soon after it reported Q3 earnings on October 30. This crash followed traffic headwinds from Google's (GOOGL) AI Overviews and the rollout of its new artificial intelligence (AI) Mode features, which negatively impacted Reddit's user growth.

However, on November 4, Reddit stock surged 6% after the company announced that it is testing ad placements on Reddit search pages. This is a major step forward in monetizing its existing user base. The company is also planning to double down on forcing non-logged-in users to create accounts and log in to the platform. I am bullish on Reddit as I believe its recently announced strategies will trigger strong earnings growth.

Reddit Is Under Threat from AI

Although I am bullish on Reddit long term, there's no denying the company faces a major challenge as search engines embrace AI answers. The biggest culprit is Google. The aggressive rollout of AI Overview and AI Mode have fundamentally changed SEO principles. As confirmed by Reddit's management, Google continues to crawl Reddit to support AI answers. However, this does not translate into any user growth for Reddit.

Commenting on this during the Q3 earnings call, CEO Steven Huffman said, "Google is crawling us as hard as ever. So the demand hasn't changed from their point of view either. The reality is: the AI Mode does not drive traffic, not for us and not to anybody as far as I know. So it's just a fundamental shift in how Google works. It used to be a traffic driver. Now it's not. So now that changes the equation for sure."

Google search referrals have historically played a big role in Reddit's user growth. The company's user acquisition funnel usually begins with a Google query, which leads to a Reddit click, which results in a non-logged-in user acquisition. Over time, Reddit converts these users into logged-in users through its appeal. This business model is now under pressure, as AI Overview and AI Mode threaten the company's user-acquisition funnel.

Reddit Is Doubling Down on Monetization

One of the reasons behind my bullish stance on Reddit despite the threat posed by AI is the company's focus on improving monetization of its active users. The company is trying to achieve this objective in two ways. First, as CEO Huffman revealed on the Q3 earnings call, Reddit is gradually transitioning to a fully logged-in-only experience. The company is initially testing this in select markets outside the United States.
